arXiv:0704.1690v1 [math.AG] 13 Apr 2007

Two Results on Homogeneous Hessian Nilpotent Polynomials

Arno van den Essen∗ and Wenhua Zhao∗∗
Abstract.

Let z=(z1,⋯,zn)z=(z_{1},\cdots,z_{n}) and Δ=∑i=1n∂2∂zi2\Delta=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial z^{2}_{i}} the Laplace operator. A formal power series P⁡(z)P(z) is said to be Hessian Nilpotent(HN) if its Hessian matrix Hes ​P​(z)=(∂2P∂zi​∂zj)\text{Hes\,}P(z)=(\frac{\partial^{2}P}{\partial z_{i}\partial z_{j}}) is nilpotent. In recent developments in [BE1], [M] and [Z], the Jacobian conjecture has been reduced to the following so-called vanishing conjecture(VC) of HN polynomials: for any homogeneous HN polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) ((of degree d=4d=4)), we have Δm​Pm+1​(z)=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}(z)=0 for any m>>0m>>0. In this paper, we first show that, the VC holds for any homogeneous HN polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) provided that the projective subvarieties 𝒵P{\mathcal{Z}}_{P} and 𝒵σ2{\mathcal{Z}}_{\sigma_{2}} of ℂ​Pn−1{\mathbb{C}}P^{n-1} determined by the principal ideals generated by P⁡(z)P(z) and σ2​(z):=∑i=1nzi2\sigma_{2}(z)\!:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}^{2}, respectively, intersect only at regular points of 𝒵P{\mathcal{Z}}_{P}. Consequently, the Jacobian conjecture holds for the symmetric polynomial maps F=z−∇PF=z-\nabla P with P⁡(z)P(z) HN if FF has no non-zero fixed point w∈ℂnw\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n} with ∑i=1nwi2=0\sum_{i=1}^{n}w_{i}^{2}=0. Secondly, we show that the VC holds for a HN formal power series P⁡(z)P(z) if and only if, for any polynomial f⁡(z)f(z), Δm​(f⁡(z)​P​(z)m)=0\Delta^{m}(f(z)P(z)^{m})=0 when m>>0m>>0.

Key words and phrases: 
Hessian nilpotent polynomials, the vanishing conjecture, symmetric polynomial maps, the Jacobian conjecture.
2000 Mathematics Subject Classification
14R15, 31B05.

1. Introduction and Main Results

Let z=(z1,z2,⋯,zn)z=(z_{1},z_{2},\cdots,z_{n}) be commutative free variables. Recall that the well-known Jacobian conjecture claims that: any polynomial map F⁡(z):ℂn→ℂnF(z):{\mathbb{C}}^{n}\to{\mathbb{C}}^{n} with the Jacobian j​(F)​(z)≡1j(F)(z)\equiv 1 is an autompophism of ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n} and its inverse map must also be a polynomial map. Despite intense study from mathematicians in more than sixty years, the conjecture is still open even for the case n=2n=2. In 1998, S. Smale [S] included the Jacobian conjecture in his list of 1818 important mathematical problems for 2121st century. For more history and known results on the Jacobian conjecture, see [BCW], [E] and references there.

Recently, M. de Bondt and the first author [BE1] and G. Meng [M] independently made the following remarkable breakthrough on the Jacobian conjecture. Namely, they reduced the Jacobian conjecture to the so-called symmetric polynomial maps, i.e the polynomial maps of the form F=z−∇PF=z-\nabla P, where ∇P:=(∂P∂z1,∂P∂z2,⋯,∂P∂zn)\nabla P\!:=(\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{1}},\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{2}},\cdots,\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{n}}), i.e. ∇P​(z)\nabla P(z) is the gradient of P⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]P(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z].

For more recent developments on the Jacobian conjecture for symmetric polynomial maps, see [BE1]–[BE4].

Based on the symmetric reduction above and also the classical homogeneous reduction in [BCW] and [Y], the second author in [Z] further reduced the Jacobian conjecture to the following so-called vanishing conjecture.

Let Δ:=∑i=1n∂2∂zi2\Delta\!:=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\frac{\partial^{2}}{\partial z^{2}_{i}} the Laplace operator and call a formal power series P⁡(z)P(z) Hessian nilpotent(HN) if its Hessian matrix Hes ​P​(z):=(∂2P∂zi​∂zj)\text{Hes\,}P(z)\!:=(\frac{\partial^{2}P}{\partial z_{i}\partial z_{j}}) is nilpotent. It has been shown in [Z] that the Jacobian conjecture is equivalent to

Conjecture 1.1.

(Vanishing Conjecture of HN Polynomials)
For any homogeneous HN polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) ((of degree d=4d=4)), we have Δm​Pm+1=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}=0 when m>>0m>>0.

Note that, it has also been shown in [Z] that P⁡(z)P(z) is HN if and only if Δm​Pm=0\Delta^{m}P^{m}=0 for m≥1m\geq 1.

In this paper, we will prove the following two results on HN polynomials.

Let P⁡(z)P(z) be a homogeneous HN polynomial of degree d≥3d\geq 3 and σ2​(z):=∑i=1nzi2\sigma_{2}(z)\!\!:=\!\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}^{2}. We denote by 𝒵P{\mathcal{Z}}_{P} and 𝒵σ2{\mathcal{Z}}_{\sigma_{2}} the projective subvarieties of ℂ​Pn−1{\mathbb{C}}P^{n-1} determined by the principal ideals generated by P⁡(z)P(z) and σ2​(z)\sigma_{2}(z), respectively. The first main result of this paper is the following theorem.

Theorem 1.2.

Let P⁡(z)P(z) be a homogeneous HN polynomial of degree d≥4d\geq 4. Assume that 𝒵P{\mathcal{Z}}_{P} intersects with 𝒵σ2{\mathcal{Z}}_{\sigma_{2}} only at regular points of 𝒵P{\mathcal{Z}}_{P}, then the vanishing conjecture holds for P⁡(z)P(z). In particular, the vanishing conjecture holds if the projective variety 𝒵P{\mathcal{Z}}_{P} is regular.

Remark 1.3.

Note that, when deg⁡P⁡(z)=d=2\deg P(z)=d=2 or 33, the Jacobian conjecture holds for the symmetric polynomial map F=z−∇PF=z-\nabla P. This is because, when d=2d=2, FF is a linear map with j⁡(F)≡1j(F)\equiv 1. Hence FF is an automorphism of ℂn{\mathbb{C}}^{n}; while when d=3d=3, we have deg⁡F=2\deg F=2. By Wang’s theorem [W], the Jacobian conjecture holds for FF again. Then, by the equivalence of the vanishing conjecture for the homogeneous HN polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) and the Jacobian conjecture for the symmetric map F=z−∇PF=z-\nabla P established in [Z], we see that, when deg⁡P⁡(z)=d=2\deg P(z)=d=2 or 33, Theorem 1.2 actually also holds even without the condition on the projective variety 𝒵P{\mathcal{Z}}_{P}.

For any non-zero z∈ℂnz\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, denote by [z][z] its image in the projective space ℂ​Pn−1{\mathbb{C}}P^{n-1}. Set

(1.1) 𝒵~σ2:={z∈ℂn|z≠0;[z]∈𝒵σ2}.\displaystyle\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{\sigma_{2}}\!:=\{z\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}\,|\,z\neq 0;\,[z]\in{\mathcal{Z}}_{\sigma_{2}}\}.

In other words, 𝒵~σ2\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{\sigma_{2}} is the set of non-zero z∈ℂnz\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n} such that ∑i=1nzi2=0\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}^{2}=0.

Note that, for any homogeneous polynomial P⁡(z)P(z) of degree dd, it follows from the Euler’s formula d​P=∑i=1nzi​d​Pd​zidP=\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}\frac{dP}{dz_{i}}, that any non-zero w∈ℂnw\in{\mathbb{C}}^{n}, [w]∈ℂ​Pn−1[w]\in{\mathbb{C}}P^{n-1} is a singular point of 𝒵P{\mathcal{Z}}_{P} if and only if ww is a fixed point of the symmetric map F=z−∇PF=z-\nabla P. Furthermore, it is also well-known that, j⁡(F)≡1j(F)\equiv 1 if and only if P⁡(z)P(z) is HN.

By the observations above and Theorem 1.2, it is easy to see that we have the following corollary on symmetric polynomial maps.

Corollary 1.4.

Let F=z−∇PF=z-\nabla P with PP homogeneous and j⁡(F)≡1j(F)\equiv 1 ((or equivalently, PP is HN)). Assume that FF does not fix any w∈𝒵~σ2w\in\widetilde{\mathcal{Z}}_{\sigma_{2}}. Then the Jacobian holds for F⁡(z)F(z). In particular, if FF has no non-zero fixed point, the Jacobian conjecture holds for FF.

Our second main result is following theorem which says that the vanishing conjecture is actually equivalent to a formally much stronger statement.

Theorem 1.5.

For any HN polynomial P⁡(z)P(z), the vanishing conjecture holds for P⁡(z)P(z) if and only if, for any polynomial f⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]f(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z], Δm​(f⁡(z)​P​(z)m)=0\Delta^{m}(f(z)P(z)^{m})=0 when m>>0m>>0.

2. Proof of the Main Results

Let us first fix the following notation. Let z=(z1,z2,⋯,zn)z=(z_{1},z_{2},\cdots,z_{n}) be free complex variables and ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z] (resp. ℂ⁡[[z]]{\mathbb{C}}[[z]]) the algebra of polynomials (resp. formal power series) in zz. For any d≥0d\geq 0, we denote by VdV_{d} the vector space of homogeneous polynomials in zz of degree dd.

For any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n, we set Di=∂∂ziD_{i}=\frac{\partial}{\partial z_{i}} and D=(D1,D2,⋯,Dn)D=(D_{1},D_{2},\cdots,D_{n}). We define a ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-bilinear map {⋅,⋅}:ℂ⁡[z]×ℂ⁡[z]→ℂ⁡[z]\{\cdot,\cdot\}:{\mathbb{C}}[z]\times{\mathbb{C}}[z]\to{\mathbb{C}}[z] by setting

{f,g}:=f⁡(D)​g​(z)\displaystyle\{f,\,g\}\!:=f(D)g(z)

for any f⁡(z),g⁡(z)∈ℂ⁡[z]f(z),g(z)\in{\mathbb{C}}[z].

Note that, for any m≥0m\geq 0, the restriction of {⋅,⋅}\{\cdot,\cdot\} on Vm×VmV_{m}\times V_{m} gives a ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-bilinear form of the vector subspace VmV_{m}, which we will denote by Bm​(⋅,⋅)B_{m}(\cdot,\cdot). It is easy to check that, for any m≥1m\geq 1, Bm​(⋅,⋅)B_{m}(\cdot,\cdot) is symmetric and non-singular.

The following lemma will play a crucial role in our proof of the first main result.

Lemma 2.1.

For any homogeneous polynomials gi​(z)g_{i}(z) (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k) of degree di≥1d_{i}\geq 1, let SS be the vector space of polynomial solutions of the following system of PDEs:

(2.2) {g1​(D)​u​(z)=0,g2​(D)​u​(z)=0,…..gk​(D)​u​(z)=0.\displaystyle\begin{cases}g_{1}(D)\,u(z)=0,\\ g_{2}(D)\,u(z)=0,\\ \quad.....\quad\\ g_{k}(D)\,u(z)=0.\end{cases}

Then, dimS<+∞\dim S<+\infty if and only if gi​(z)g_{i}(z) (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k) have no non-zero common zeroes.

Proof:  Let II the homogeneous ideal of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z] generated by {gi​(z)|1≤i≤k}\{g_{i}(z)|1\leq i\leq k\}. Since all gi​(z)g_{i}(z)’s are homogeneous, SS is a homogeneous vector subspace SS of ℂ⁡[z]{\mathbb{C}}[z].

Write

(2.3) S\displaystyle S =⨁m=0∞Sm,\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{m=0}^{\infty}S_{m},
(2.4) I\displaystyle I =⨁m=0∞Im.\displaystyle=\bigoplus_{m=0}^{\infty}I_{m}.

where Im:=I∩VmI_{m}\!:=I\cap V_{m} and Sm:=I∩VmS_{m}\!:=I\cap V_{m} for any m≥0m\geq 0.

Claim: For any m≥1m\geq 1 and u⁡(z)∈Vmu(z)\in V_{m}, u⁡(z)∈Smu(z)\in S_{m} if and only if {u,Im}=0\{u,I_{m}\}=0, or in other words, Sm=Im⟂S_{m}=I_{m}^{\perp} with respect to the ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-bilinear form Bm​(⋅,⋅)B_{m}(\cdot,\cdot) of VmV_{m}.

Proof of the Claim: First, by the definitions of II and SS, we have {Im,Sm}=0\{I_{m},S_{m}\}=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1, hence Sm⊆Im⟂S_{m}\subseteq I_{m}^{\perp}. Therefore, we need only show that, for any u⁡(z)∈Im⟂⊂Vmu(z)\in I_{m}^{\perp}\subset V_{m}, gi​(D)​u​(z)=0g_{i}(D)u(z)=0 for any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n.

We first fix any 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. If m<dim<d_{i}, there is nothing to prove. If m=dim=d_{i}, then gi​(z)∈Img_{i}(z)\in I_{m}, hence {gi,u}=gi​(D)​u=0\{g_{i},u\}=g_{i}(D)u=0. Now suppose m>dim>d_{i}. Note that, for any v⁡(z)∈Vm−div(z)\in V_{m-d_{i}}, v⁡(z)​gi​(z)∈Imv(z)g_{i}(z)\in I_{m}. Hence we have

0\displaystyle 0 ={v⁡(z)​gi​(z),u⁡(z)}\displaystyle=\{v(z)g_{i}(z),u(z)\}
=v⁡(D)​gi​(D)​u​(z)\displaystyle=v(D)g_{i}(D)u(z)
=v⁡(D)​(gi​(D)​u)​(z)\displaystyle=v(D)\left(g_{i}(D)u\right)(z)
={v⁡(z),(gi​(D)​u)​(z)}.\displaystyle=\{v(z),\left(g_{i}(D)u\right)(z)\}.

Therefore, we have

Bm−di​((gi​(D)​u)​(z),Vm−di)=0.B_{m-d_{i}}\left((g_{i}(D)u)(z),\,V_{m-d_{i}}\right)=0.

Since Bm−di​(⋅,⋅)B_{m-d_{i}}(\cdot,\cdot) is a non-singular ℂ{\mathbb{C}}-bilinear form of Vm−diV_{m-d_{i}}, we have gi​(D)​u=0g_{i}(D)u=0. Hence, the Claim holds.  □\Box

By a well-known fact in Algebraic Geometry (see Exercise 2.22.2 in [H], for example), we know that the homogeneous polynomials gi​(z)g_{i}(z) (1≤i≤k)(1\leq i\leq k) have no non-zero common zeroes if and only if Im=VmI_{m}=V_{m} when m>>0m>>0. While, by the Claim above, we know that, Im=VmI_{m}=V_{m} when m>>0m>>0 if and only if Sm=0S_{m}=0 when m>>0m>>0, and if and only if the solution space SS of the system (2.2) is finite dimensional. Hence, the lemma follows.  □\Box

Now we are ready to prove our first main result, Theorem 1.2.

Proof of Theorem 1.2: Let P⁡(z)P(z) be a homogeneous HN polynomial of degree d≥4d\geq 4 and SS the vector space of polynomial solutions of the following system of PDEs:

(2.5) {∂P∂z1​(D)​u​(z)=0,∂P∂z2​(D)​u​(z)=0,…..∂P∂zn​(D)​u​(z)=0,Δ​u​(z)=0.\displaystyle\begin{cases}\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{1}}(D)\,u(z)=0,\\ \frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{2}}(D)\,u(z)=0,\\ \quad.....\quad\\ \frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{n}}(D)\,u(z)=0,\\ \Delta\,u(z)=0.\end{cases}

First, note that the projective subvariety 𝒵P{\mathcal{Z}}_{P} intersects with 𝒵σ2{\mathcal{Z}}_{\sigma_{2}} only at regular points of 𝒵P{\mathcal{Z}}_{P} if and only if ∂P∂zi​(z)\frac{\partial P}{\partial z_{i}}(z) (1≤i≤n)(1\leq i\leq n) and σ2=∑i=1nzi2\sigma_{2}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}z_{i}^{2} have no non-zero common zeros (agian use Euler’s formula). Then, by Lemma 2.1, we have dimS<+∞\dim S<+\infty.

On the other hand, by Theorem 6.36.3 in [Z], we know that Δm​Pm+1∈S\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}\in S for any m≥0m\geq 0. Note that deg⁡Δm​Pm+1=(d−2)​m+d\deg\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}=(d-2)m+d for any m≥0m\geq 0. So deg⁡Δm​Pm+1>deg⁡Δk​Pk+1\deg\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}>\deg\Delta^{k}P^{k+1} for any m>km>k. Since dimS<+∞\dim S<+\infty (from above), we have Δm​Pm+1=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+1}=0 when m>>0m>>0, i.e. the vanishing conjecture holds for P⁡(z)P(z).  □\Box

Next, we give a proof for our second main result, Theorem 1.5.

Proof of Theorem 1.5: The (⇐)(\Leftarrow) part follows directly by choosing f⁡(z)f(z) to be P⁡(z)P(z) itself.

To show (⇒)(\Rightarrow) part, let d=deg⁡f⁡(z)d=\deg f(z). If d=0d=0, ff is a constant. Then, Δm​(f⁡(z)​P​(z)m)=f⁡(z)​Δm​Pm=0\Delta^{m}(f(z)P(z)^{m})=f(z)\Delta^{m}P^{m}=0 for any m≥1m\geq 1.

So we assume d≥1d\geq 1. By Theorem 6.26.2 in [Z], we know that, if the vanishing conjecture holds for P⁡(z)P(z), then, for any fixed a≥1a\geq 1, Δm​Pm+a=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+a}=0 when m>>0m>>0. Therefore there exists N>0N>0 such that, for any 0≤b≤d0\leq b\leq d and any m>Nm>N, we have Δm​Pm+b=0\Delta^{m}P^{m+b}=0.

By Lemma 6.56.5 in [Z], for any m≥1m\geq 1, we have

(2.6) Δm​(f⁡(z)​P​(z)m)=\displaystyle\Delta^{m}(f(z)P(z)^{m})=
∑k1+k2+k3=mk1,k2,k3≥02k2​(mk1,k2,k3)​∑𝐬∈ℕn|𝐬|=k2(k2𝐬)​∂k2Δk1​f​(z)∂z𝐬​∂k2Δk3​Pm​(z)∂z𝐬,\displaystyle\,\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3}=m\\ k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}\geq 0\end{subarray}}2^{k_{2}}\binom{m}{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}{\bf s}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{n}\\ |{\bf s}|=k_{2}\end{subarray}}\binom{k_{2}}{\bf s}\frac{\partial^{k_{2}}\Delta^{k_{1}}f(z)}{\partial z^{\bf s}}\frac{\partial^{k_{2}}\Delta^{k_{3}}P^{m}(z)}{\partial z^{\bf s}},

where (mk1,k2,k3)\binom{m}{k_{1},k_{2},k_{3}} and (k2𝐬)\binom{k_{2}}{\bf s} denote the usual binomials.

Note first that, the general term in the sum above is non-zero only if 2​k1+k2≤d2k_{1}+k_{2}\leq d. But on the other hand, since

(2.7) 0≤k1+k2≤2​k1+k2≤d,\displaystyle 0\leq k_{1}+k_{2}\leq 2k_{1}+k_{2}\leq d,

by the choice of N≥1N\geq 1, we have Δk3​Pm​(z)=Δk3​Pk3+(k1+k2)​(z)\Delta^{k_{3}}P^{m}(z)=\Delta^{k_{3}}P^{k_{3}+(k_{1}+k_{2})}(z) is non-zero only if

(2.8) k3≤N.\displaystyle k_{3}\leq N.

From the observations above and Eqs. (2.6), (2.7), (2.8) it is easy to see that, Δm​(f⁡(z)​P​(z)m)≠0\Delta^{m}(f(z)P(z)^{m})\neq 0 only if m=k1+k2+k3≤d+Nm=k_{1}+k_{2}+k_{3}\leq d+N. In other words, Δm​(f⁡(z)​P​(z)m)=0\Delta^{m}(f(z)P(z)^{m})=0 for any m>d+Nm>d+N. Hence Theorem 1.5 holds.  □\Box

Note that all results used in the proof above for the (⇐)(\Leftarrow) part of the theorem also hold for all HN formal power series. Therefore we have the following corollary.

Corollary 2.2.

Let P⁡(z)P(z) be a HN formal power series such that the vanishing conjecture holds for P⁡(z)P(z). Then, for any polynomial f⁡(z)f(z), we have Δm​(f⁡(z)​P​(z)m)=0\Delta^{m}(f(z)P(z)^{m})=0 when m>>0m>>0.
